title: Switching From QuickBooks to Construction-Specific Accounting Software: What Actually Changes
summary: What changes when contractors move from QuickBooks to construction-specific accounting software, covering job costing, certified payroll, and compliance.
body_markdown:
Most contractors start with QuickBooks. The software is affordable, widely understood, and handles core accounting tasks well enough for a company running a handful of projects. But at some point, the workarounds start piling up: spreadsheets tracking job costs that QuickBooks cannot break down by phase and cost code, manual certified payroll reports assembled outside the system, and retainage calculations that live in Excel because the accounting software has no native way to hold and release them.


The question is not whether QuickBooks is good software. For general small business accounting, it is. The question is whether a platform built for retail stores, consulting firms, and freelancers can handle the financial complexity of a growing trade contractor managing multiple job sites, prevailing wage obligations, union reporting, and compliance documentation across states.


## **Where QuickBooks Hits Its Limits for Contractors**


QuickBooks handles invoicing, bank reconciliation, and basic financial reporting well. The gaps show up in construction-specific workflows that the software was never designed to support natively.


### **Job Costing**


Job costing is the financial backbone of a construction business. Every dollar of labor, material, and equipment needs to be traced to a specific project, phase, and cost code so the contractor can see whether a job is making or losing money in real time.


QuickBooks offers a basic Projects feature that tracks income and expenses by job. What it does not offer is the layered cost code structure that construction accounting requires. A contractor managing a concrete scope on a commercial project needs to separate labor, formwork, rebar, and finishing costs within a single job, then compare actual spend against the original estimate at each level. QuickBooks was not built for that depth, and contractors who try to force it end up maintaining parallel spreadsheets to get the visibility they need.


### **Certified Payroll and Prevailing Wage**


Contractors working on public projects must submit[certified payroll](https://www.buildtrayd.com/solution/compliance/certified-payroll) reports verifying that workers were paid the correct prevailing wage rates. QuickBooks does not produce certified payroll reports natively. Generating a WH-347 or state-equivalent form requires third-party add-ons or manual assembly outside the system.


Prevailing wage rate management is similarly limited. On a public project with multiple trade classifications, each governed by a different hourly rate and fringe benefit schedule, contractors need payroll systems that can apply the correct rate per worker, per classification, per project. QuickBooks Payroll can handle multiple pay rates, but managing prevailing wage compliance across several active projects with different wage determinations quickly exceeds what the platform was designed to do.


### **Retainage, AIA Billing, and Change Orders**


Three construction-specific financial workflows that QuickBooks handles poorly or not at all:


-


**Retainage:** On most commercial and public construction contracts, the owner withholds a percentage of each payment (typically 5–10%) until the project reaches substantial completion. Tracking retainage receivable and retainage payable requires dedicated accounts and release schedules that QuickBooks does not manage natively.


-


**AIA billing:** Progress billing using AIA G702/G703 forms is standard on commercial construction projects. QuickBooks has no built-in support for percentage-of-completion billing, scheduled values, or the continuation sheet format that project owners and general contractors expect.


-


**Change orders:** Modifications to the original contract scope affect budgets, billing, and job cost projections. QuickBooks has no native change order tracking, so contractors manage them in separate documents and manually update financial records.


## **What Construction-Specific Software Does Differently**


A platform built for construction does not add construction features on top of a generic accounting engine. The entire data structure is designed around how contractors actually earn, spend, and report money.


### **Integrated Job Cost Accounting**


Construction-specific accounting software organises the general ledger around jobs rather than departments. Every transaction, whether a payroll entry, a vendor invoice, or a material purchase, ties to a project, phase, and cost code. Real-time budget-versus-actual reporting at the cost code level gives project managers and controllers visibility into job profitability without manual data assembly.


A ​[construction job costing](https://www.buildtrayd.com/solution/job-costing/construction-job-costing) platform that connects labor data from the field to the financial ledger eliminates the gap between what was spent and what the accounting system reflects.


### **Native Compliance Reporting**


Construction accounting platforms produce certified payroll reports, WIP (Work in Progress) schedules, and union fringe benefit reports as standard outputs, not add-ons. When ​[construction payroll](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll) and compliance reporting share the same data source, the back office does not rebuild certified payroll from scratch each week. The report pulls directly from verified timecard and payroll data.


### **Accounts Payable Built for Subcontractor Management**


A contractor's ​[accounts payable](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/accounting/accounts-payable-receivable) workflow involves far more than processing vendor invoices. Subcontractor payments require lien waiver tracking, retainage holds, compliance verification (COIs, W-9s, certified payroll), and job-coded cost allocation. Construction-specific AP ties every payment to a project and cost code, and connects compliance documentation to the payment approval workflow.


## **What the Transition Actually Looks Like**


Switching accounting platforms is a significant operational change for any business, and contractors should plan for it rather than treat it as a weekend project.


### **Data Migration**


The historical data in QuickBooks needs to move to the new platform. Chart of accounts, vendor and customer lists, open invoices, job history, and payroll records all require mapping to the new system's structure. Most construction software vendors have handled thousands of QuickBooks migrations and can advise on what to bring forward and what to leave behind.


### **The Learning Curve**


Staff members who have used QuickBooks for years will need time to learn the new system. Construction-specific software is more powerful, but power comes with complexity. Plan for a training period and expect a temporary dip in productivity before the team reaches full speed.


### **When the Switch Makes Sense**


Several signals indicate that a contractor has outgrown QuickBooks:


-


Managing five or more concurrent projects with meaningful ​[job costing](https://www.buildtrayd.com/solution/job-costing/construction-job-costing) requirements


-


Performing public or prevailing wage work that requires certified ​[payroll reports](https://www.buildtrayd.com/products/payroll/construction-payroll-reports)


-


Tracking retainage across multiple active contracts


-


Running multi-state operations with different tax and compliance rules


-


Spending more time building workarounds in spreadsheets than using the accounting software


None of these individually force a migration, but the combination creates operational drag that compounds as the company grows.

## **Frequently Asked Questions**


### Can QuickBooks handle certified payroll for construction?


QuickBooks does not produce certified payroll reports natively. Contractors on prevailing wage projects typically need third-party add-ons or manual processes to generate WH-347 or state-equivalent forms.


### What is the biggest limitation of QuickBooks for contractors?


Job costing depth is the most common constraint. QuickBooks can track costs by project, but lacks the phase and cost code structure that construction accounting requires for budget-versus-actual reporting at a granular level.


### How long does it take to switch from QuickBooks to construction software?


Timelines vary by company size and data complexity. Most migrations take several weeks to a few months, including data migration, system configuration, and staff training.


### Do I need construction-specific software if I only do residential work?


Small residential contractors with a few active projects can often operate in QuickBooks. Once the business grows beyond five or six concurrent jobs, or takes on commercial or public work, construction-specific software typically becomes necessary.


### What data moves from QuickBooks to a new system?


Chart of accounts, vendor and customer lists, open invoices, job history, and payroll records are the primary data elements. Most construction software vendors have established migration processes for QuickBooks data.


### Does switching from QuickBooks mean losing my accountant's familiarity?


Many construction CPAs and bookkeepers already work with platforms like Foundation, Sage, and other construction-specific systems. The transition often improves collaboration because the software produces reports (WIP schedules, job cost summaries) that construction accountants expect.
